title: Fallback-loop from inconsistent variant mapping — incident postmortem and remediation
creator: Aisha Patel
description: Summary: On 2026-01-18 we observed a multi-region cascade where customer requests experienced sudden latency spikes and elevated error rates. Root cause was an inconsistency between the routing layer's variant compatibility table and the model-serving inventory: routing favored a cheaper 'quantized' variant without validating that the selected GPU pool had the necessary kernels available. Requests routed to that variant failed validation at the endpoint, triggered automatic fallback to a non-ideal variant, which then caused further fallbacks and cross-region reroutes. This produced a feedback loop that amplified load on healthy pools and caused tail latency increases and transient 5xx errors for affected customers. This ticket documents detection, timeline, root cause, remediation, and follow-ups.
detection: Alerting: two dashboards alerted simultaneously: per-region p95 latency (dashboard: /dashboards/routing/latency-by-region) and fallback-rate (metric: routing.fallback.rate). PagerDuty page triggered at 2026-01-18T09:22Z. Incident started when fallback-rate exceeded 4% for region-us-west-2 and p95 latency rose above 800ms for external-hosted tier routes.
timeline:
2026-01-18T09:05Z — first anomalous increase in KV-cache hit ratio for quantized variants observed in us-west-2.
2026-01-18T09:12Z — routing service propagated a drain intent for a subset of us-west-2 GPU pools (triggered by capacity reclaim job).
2026-01-18T09:18Z — router began preferring fallback mapping to quantized variant due to cost-tier rule; compatibility check skipped due to an optimization change in routing v1.21.
2026-01-18T09:22Z — endpoint validation for quantized variant failed for ~60% of routed requests (runtime rejected with error 422: kernel-mismatch).
2026-01-18T09:23Z — automatic fallback kicked in: router retried to alternative variant in another region, adding cross-region network latency and duplicating load.
2026-01-18T09:30Z — cascading effect caused surge in p95 across adjacent regions; on-call team started mitigation steps (disable quantized preference and throttle fallbacks).
2026-01-18T09:45Z — temporary patch deployed: routing policy updated to require endpoint compatibility handshake before switching variants (hotfix GH#4321).
2026-01-18T10:05Z — metrics trending back toward baseline; incident declared mitigated at 2026-01-18T10:20Z.
2026-01-25 — postmortem analysis completed and remediation tasks tracked in this ticket.
impact: Approximately 12% of live traffic for affected paid customers in us-west-2 experienced increased latency (p95 up to 1200ms) and an aggregated 3.4% increase in error surface (5xx and 422). No customer data loss; highest-impact customers were mid-market tenants using hosted-tier models with quantization enabled. Billing was unaffected but several customers reported degraded UX and opened support tickets.
root_cause: A three-part failure chain: (1) a routing optimization (v1.21) intentionally removed a synchronous variant compatibility check to reduce per-request latency, relying on an eventually-consistent 'variant_capabilities' cache; (2) a concurrent capacity drain operation marked specific GPU pools as draining but did not update the inventory's kernel availability flags in time; (3) the routing policy prioritized cost-tier mapping to quantized variants when capacity fell below threshold. The combination meant routing could select a variant that was not actually compatible with the chosen GPU pool, causing the endpoint to reject requests and triggering fallback retries. Those retries were not rate-limited and could trigger cross-region reroutes, creating a positive feedback loop.
remediation:
Short-term (hotfix): reintroduce a synchronous compatibility handshake in the router before committing a route (deployed GH#4321). Added a soft circuit breaker to limit fallback retries per request (default 1 additional region).
Medium-term: (1) reconcile variant_capabilities cache through stronger invalidation and a periodic refresh job; (2) add preflight kernel-availability checks in the capacity drain workflow so draining pools update inventory immediately; (3) update routing policy to prefer same-region compatible fallbacks and to include a compatibility score in routing decisions.
Long-term: introduce a model-variant compatibility contract with the serving runtime (API versioning) so mismatches can be detected at build/deploy time rather than at runtime.
follow_up_tasks: ENG-9072: Implement periodic full refresh for variant_capabilities cache (estimate 5)
ENG-9081: Add kernel-availability update hook to drain workflow (estimate 3)
ENG-9090: Routing policy change — compatibility score and same-region preference (estimate 8)
ENG-9102: Create canary and chaos tests for fallback behavior under drain (SRE lead) (estimate 5)
ENG-9110: Update runbook and incident playbook for fallback floods (docs) (estimate 2)
monitoring: New alerts added: routing.compatibility.failure.rate > 0.5% sustained for 2m; routing.fallback.cross-region.rate > 0.2% for 5m. Dashboards updated: 'fallback waterfall' to show origin variant -> attempted fallback variants -> final outcome. We also added sampling traces in the router to capture the decision tree for 1% of requests when a fallback occurs.
comments: 2026-01-18 10:30 — Mateo Alvarez: Hotfix GH#4321 deployed. Reintroduced synchronous compatibility check and added fallback throttle. Early telemetry looks good. Moving to monitoring. (assigned follow-ups)
2026-01-19 09:12 — SRE: Observed that the drain job does not call inventory.invalidate() in the edge case where host reclaim was concurrent. Added a short-term cron to reconcile inventory (testing).
2026-01-20 14:05 — PM (Lina Moore): Need to inform affected customers with a summary and mitigation steps. Drafted a message to sent to account team.
2026-01-22 11:40 — Eng Lead (Ravi Menon): Recommend pursuing the compatibility contract as a high-priority engineering initiative. Prioritize ENG-9072 and ENG-9081 in next cycle.
2026-01-24 16:18 — Security (Jenna Yoon): No sensitive data exposure detected. Confirmed that fallback throttles do not alter auth semantics.
notes: Lessons learned: optimistic performance optimizations that remove validation must be gated behind stronger invariants (cache invalidation, contract guarantees). Fallbacks are a safety net but can amplify problems if not rate-limited or compatibility-aware. Immediate wins were the compatibility handshake and fallback rate limits; medium-term durability requires inventory-driven guarantees and stronger coordination between drain workflows and routing caches.
